During my last deployment while I was in the Navy the ship made a port call at Hurghada, Egypt in the Red Sea. The ship was anchored off-shore and we were using small boats between the ship and shore. The pier we disembarked at was also used by large boats that served European tourists on excursions.

I watched while one of those boats was replenishing stores. Egyptian workers busy carrying baskets and boxes of vegetables and grains from a couple of pickup trucks onto the boat. Then came a couple trucks with the livestock. Chickens, a couple of sheep, and a cow were wrestled off the trucks, killed, butchered and the carcasses loaded aboard.

 I found it interesting that the only ones affected by the event were the other sailors I was with, some of whom raced to the edge of the pier to vomit. Their reaction drew far more attention from the locals than the butchering did. A German tourist asked me if there was something wrong with them. My answer was that they just found out where their burgers and chicken nuggets came from.

Just goes to show how insulated Americans are and how little thought they give to where their food comes from. Humans have been killing animals for food for millennia. How else can we feed 300 million without doing it on an industrial scale?

Colleges and universities use Title IX investigations to protect their brand.  Title IX officers and faculty review committees are not trained in sexual assault investigation, evidence collection, impartial interrogation, and the dynamics of sexual trauma or PTSD.  And a horrible by-product of unqualified Title IX interviews, even if the officials are well meaning, is that they muddy or flat out interfere with criminal investigations.  Title IX isn’t designed to reach a factual result.  It is designed to make sure all parties -  innocent, guilty, or honestly mistaken - feel “safe” and “heard.”  And to cover the institution’s reputation.

I would never tell a victim to complain to a Title IX office.  If a victim wants an investigation, go to the police directly and (hopefully) they are properly trained in sexual assault investigation.  Police should refer a complainant to a local sexual assault resource agency.  Most importantly, even if a victim doesn’t want to report to police or go through the criminal process, they should go get a SAFE/SANE exam (sexual assault forensic nurse exam).  It’s the victim’s decision if hospital calls police, but medically at least they get support services.

Today we are witnessing inhumane acts of persecution in the US and across the globe. If my assumptions are valid, I think it may be okay for the LW to talk to her friend about what happened and ask what she can tell her about how she was feeling during the episode.  However, I am not sure what good would be served by telling her friend how much she hurt the LW.  The point should be to help her friend, not elicit an apology for having a downturn.

The caveat is that she first talk to her friend's husband and / or other members of her family, in general terms, about what she intends to do to try to ensure that whatever action she takes is more likely to make things better than worse.  However much helping her friend has hurt the LW, we can be sure that it is hurting her family more.  The LW needs to think about the consequences for her friend and her friend's family, not just for herself.  She can withdraw, They cannot.  

When dealing with someone who is suffering from mental illness, I have found that it helped me to remember that no one suffers more from their illness than they do.

While the friend may or may not recall her manic behaviors, she knows she has a severe relapsing illness. Is it harmful to tell the friend about the care she received while ill? 

Years ago, when I attended a weeklong therapy for PTSD, they reminded us - your family has been suffering, too, and as you recover, they will be happy for you, but they will also need time and space to begin to acknowledge their own experience and impact of your illness. Our job was to allow them this processing without feeling ashamed and defensive of our illness- and also, accepting culpability for behaviors that hurt them (because, as other commenters have pointed out, you can have mental illness and also be a jerk sometimes). 

In this case, I think the supportive friend needs to have her efforts acknowledge, and I think that is morally and ethically required for the friendship to move forward. Not speaking truth will sow resentment. No one can what say proportion of the false pregnancy was mania / manipulation, so this can’t be the point of the conversation. Something like: here are the ways I supported you and here are the actions I took on your behalf while you were ill. Regardless of the response to this (defensiveness, denial, gratitude, deflection etc etc), the writer has spoken their truth, and can now decide what their involvement will be next time, and / or how close they wish this relationship to remain.

Deliberate manipulation? Maybe, maybe not. 
Persons with these illnesses can be very convincing, especially to those with limited experience dealing with or recognizing  episodic behavior.
The manic friend at that moment believes in or is fully vested in their delusion. They can appear and act what seems to be quite normal considering their "crisis".
When the crisis passes there will be a new construct that integrates or ignores what has just happened.
Well meaning "friends" often have no idea what they are dealing with and even with the best intentions make things much worse.
Difficult work: try guiding your children through this.
Advice: if you are close enough to the spouse or family ask them what you can do to help, listen to them, then do what they ask you to do.
If you can't do that or are not close to the family, stay out of the situation, you are not helping.

Whether cancer, mental health or injury issues the public will in general be empathetic. Also for the individual, not keeping their health issue a secret may be freeing.

comments.name: Harris
comments.body:
I am certain that only journalists and other members of the media care about any of these supposedly urgent questions.

Why wouldn't the pope or any of his spokesmen wait until the actual biopsy confirmed the cancer diagnosis to announce it?

I'm not Catholic but even I understand that the significance of Lourdes is not only in the solace it gives the sick.

I am saddened that this vibrant, admirable pope has to face the uncertainty ahead of him but I am confident that he will be transparent with us as events proceed.

May we give 'the man' more than a week to deal with what has just happened to him?

'The Pope' will do just fine as soon as 'the man' is ready.

comments.name: FCP
comments.body:
I disagree with the comments that claim the Vatican has been “ transparent”. 

There is nothing transparent about announcing the diagnosis only after the surgery was completed. They knew it was cancer after the PET scan, and certainly after the bronchoscopy under general anesthesia. Only now are we hearing he had this invasive and unusual procedure. 

We still do not know why he had a CT scan in the first place, as this is not usual care for a non smoker.

comments.name: Been There Experienced this
comments.body: Cancer is not the death sentence it used to be. He has been honest ion his own time schedule. Having been given a cancer diagnosis, I know it takes a little bit to understand that and accept it. He told us when he was ready. I don’t see a problem with that.

comments.name: Jessica
comments.body: The man deserves his privacy during his healing. Pope's have come and gone. The world hasn't ended with any of them passing. Morbid curiosity loses this one.

articles.title: Uncertainty Over Pope’s Health Fuels Familiar Debate Over Vatican’s Candor
articles.summary: By announcing his lung condition himself, Leo has been more forthcoming than many popes. But mysteries remain, prompting scrutiny of papal statements for hidden meaning.

comments.name: stephan morrow
comments.body:
We are so ready to shift in our pts of view. Imagine if she would have encountered one like those poor souls after the Indianapolis sank. 'She's so hungry'. Not when it's chewing your leg. Different if it was a dolphin who can also be pretty vicious. When I landed on Oahu in from Japan and got a job in Sea Life Park a young dolphin was sick and the locals who were wearing ski parkas – to them it was winter while to me it felt like summer – I dove in and swam him back to the tank's edge (I used a lifeguard technique - by his pectoral fins). Til then I had been treated like 'the outsider' but it was great to be the 'hero of the day'. Until another young male was brought in and the older bull objected to the competition for his harem. Next AM the young one was floating in the tank with contusions all over him. (don't think I realized what an honor it was - but I was invited to assist in the autopsy). But the Nordic (chilly up til then) woman was so traumatized she either resigned or was fired after that. So was I (I didn't realize she was my protector). So back to the beach at Waimanalo. Just another traveling adventure. Please Note: I turned 21 in Pusan as a guest of a Viet Nam vet even tho I was a Soldier of Peace. Such a kind family – even tho the Koreans were known as brutal in Viet Nam.

comments.name: Ann
comments.body: What a fantastic review and characterization of the dilemmas often presented in life -- where reality is not just one lived experience but many events; some that put us in conflict with our imagined or interpretations of experience and what actually is. Risk, grief, contradictions saying "yes" even when the heart is shattered, when pain and loss seems never ending. Wow!
